# Synthesis

Field's own signal graph — the part of the audio stack that makes samples rather than arranging them. One value type carries the whole thing: `Signal` is a block-rendered mono source, `SignalProcessor` is a `Signal` that reads another one, and `/` chains the two, so `saw / OnePole(800.p)` is a filtered sawtooth and nothing else had to be declared. Control values are `Param`, which a plain number becomes with `.p`, and which can itself be driven by a signal. `audio { … }` closes a mono or stereo graph into an `AudioPatchSpec`; return one as a box's last expression and the box stays lit for as long as it is making sound. Underneath is a shared OpenAL engine, one process-wide, with warm-up passes available so the first buffer is not also the JIT's first look at your graph. On top of the oscillator / filter / effect / envelope families sit three larger things that are not Field's own DSP: **Faust**, whose compiler is embedded as WebAssembly and turns a `#faust` box into a running node in the same graph; the **dough** ports, hand-rolled float math whose inaccuracy is part of the sound; and the **spectral** and **granular** layers, which are Field's own. `Visualizers.kt` is how you look at any of it — every function there is an extension on a type declared in this category. Start from `synth.kt`, which is the terse surface a box actually imports; [Sound: from a pattern to something you can hear](../sound.md) is the prose, [Faust](../faust.md) is the embedded compiler with worked examples, and [DoughDSP: hear the primitives](../dough_dsp_sound.md) plays the ports.

## CsoundInstance.kt { #csoundinstance-kt }

A running Csound you can render offline or play through Field's audio engine, with queued score
events, live recompilation and thread-safe control channels.

### CsoundNode { #csoundinstance-kt-csoundnode }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">CsoundNode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">csound</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">CsoundInstance</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">input</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StereoRenderable</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">audioIn</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Map</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">String</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">afield</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">audio</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">synth</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Signal</span><span class="p">&gt;</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nf">emptyMap</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">StereoNode</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/csound/CsoundInstance/#L845)

A [`CsoundInstance`](synthesis.md#csoundinstance-kt-csoundinstance) in Field's audio graph. A [`StereoNode`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereonode) because Csound is stateful: the node's per-block cache keeps a graph that reuses it from performing twice. Whatever thread renders the graph — the audio thread, live — becomes the thread that runs Csound's perform loop, and the only thread that touches its audio.

## PdInstance.kt { #pdinstance-kt }

A running libpd instance as a Field object: [`PdInstance`](synthesis.md#pdinstance-kt-pdinstance) opens patches, renders them offline or as a [`PdNode`](synthesis.md#pdinstance-kt-pdnode) in a synth graph, and passes messages in and out.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/pd/PdInstance.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/pd/PdInstance/)

## AudioReturnValue.kt { #audioreturnvalue-kt }

The step between a box whose last expression is a patch and a patch you can hear.

`audio { … }` builds an [`AudioPatchSpec`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-audiopatchspec) and stops there, holding no device and making no sound.
This file is the other half: a return-value handler that recognises an [`AudioPatchSpec`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-audiopatchspec), a bare
[`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) or a [`StereoRenderable`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereorenderable) coming back from a box, registers it with [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) so
it joins the mix, and unregisters it when the box stops. The two bare forms are wrapped with
`AudioPatchSpec.from` first, so returning an oscillator and returning a patch built around one
reach the same place.

What the handler launches is a coroutine that mostly yields. Being cancellable is the work: it is
registered as one of the box's jobs, it re-checks the box's run generation on every pass, and it
closes the engine handle in a `finally`. A re-run therefore silences the previous patch instead
of stacking a second copy of it on top.

The same loop redraws the box's inline output. When box execution has marked the returned value's
line as an inline summary target, the loop pushes the patch's `summaryHtml`, a waveform and a
spectrum drawn from its own rolling trace, back to the editor twelve times a second, beginning
120 ms after the launch.

## Buf.kt { #buf-kt }

Bulk float-array arithmetic for the synthesis graph, written against the Java Vector API.

A [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) renders into a `FloatArray` a block at a time, 512 frames by default, so the unit of
work in this package is a few hundred samples rather than one. [`Buf`](synthesis.md#buf-kt-buf) is where that inner loop
lives: fills and copies, buffer-by-buffer and buffer-by-scalar arithmetic, fused multiply-add,
clamp and absolute value, the peak, RMS and sum reductions, a Hann window and a cross-fade.
`Signal`, `Sampling`, `Filters`, `FM`, `Envelopes`, `Spectral`, `FaustDsp` and
[`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine)'s mix loop all go through it.

Each function takes its destination first and an `off`/`len` pair last, defaulting to the whole
array from `off`. Every caller in the package passes `0` and the current block's frame count,
because the buffers grow to the largest block asked for so far and never shrink: `len` is the
live prefix, not the array's size. The vectorised functions step by `LANES` for as long as a full
vector remains and finish the rest in a scalar tail loop, so no length is a special case. Nothing
here allocates an array. Destinations are written in place, and the three reductions return a
`Float`.

Three of the functions are not vectorised: `copy` is `System.arraycopy`, and `hann` and
`hannWindow` evaluate a cosine per sample in a plain loop.

Two of them have a guard or a convention that the signature does not show. `div` returns 0 where
the divisor's magnitude is at or below `epsilon`, 1e-15 by default, rather than an infinity or a
NaN. `rms` divides the sum of squares by `len`, the window it was asked for, rather than by the
length of the array.

## CsoundBox.kt { #csoundbox-kt }

The box-facing side of Csound: an orchestra and a score as a sound source, with control channels
both ways.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val cs = csound("""
chn_k "freq", 1, 2, 220, 55, 880
instr 1
  kf chnget "freq"
  a1 vco2 0.1, kf
  outs a1, a1
endin
""", "i1 0 z")
csoundControls(cs)
cs
```

Returning the [`CsoundLaunch`](synthesis.md#csoundbox-kt-csoundlaunch) as the box's last expression is what makes it sound: it joins
[`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) as a [`afield.audio.csound.CsoundNode`](synthesis.md#csoundinstance-kt-csoundnode), so Csound's perform loop runs on the audio
thread and nowhere else, and stopping the box stops the sound and frees the Csound. What Csound
prints goes to the box's output; a compile error is marked on the box's own line.

Every launch is its own Csound, so two boxes can both use `chnget "freq"` without hearing each
other. libcsound is an optional native library; see [`CsoundLibrary`](audio.md#csoundnative-kt-csoundlibrary).

## Dough.kt { #dough-kt }

dough itself, run as WebAssembly inside GraalVM, and the two wrappers that hand its output to
Field's audio engine.

[`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) loads `dough.wasm` into a polyglot context and drives it through a small JavaScript
shim: events go in as slash-separated key/value paths, the module's `dsp()` is called one 128-frame
block at a time, and the samples are read back out of wasm memory. This is dough's own voice
allocator, event parser, filters and effects rather than a reimplementation of them. `DoughDsp.kt`
is the separate Kotlin port of a handful of dough's primitives, and the two paths never meet.

The engine does not know where its own buffers are until the module tells it. `dough_init` calls
back into `js_init` once with a query-string-shaped mirror of its pointers, which is where
`event_input`, `output`, `frame`, `framebuffer`, `pcm` and `active_voices` all come from. A pointer
the module does not report is not an error: `currentFrame` and `activeVoices` answer null, and
`framebufferCopy` answers an empty array.

Two properties shape everything built on this. A polyglot context holding `js` admits **one
thread**, so whichever thread constructs a [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) is the only one that may call any of its
methods, `activeVoices` included; GraalVM refuses a second thread rather than serialising it. And
the shim imports nothing but the memory, `js_panic` and `js_init`, so the guest has no host clock
and no host randomness: the same events and the same number of `renderBlock` calls give the same
floats, run after run, with no tolerance needed to compare two runs.

[`DoughAudioSink`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughaudiosink) is the engine wrapped as a [`StereoNode`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereonode), with commands queued rather than applied
so that a caller never reaches the engine itself, and at most `maxCommandsPerRender` of them drained
per block. It renders in whole 128-frame blocks and copies only the frames it was asked for, so a
request that is not a multiple of 128 drops the tail of its last block, which is a gap in the sound
rather than a delay in it; [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine)'s 512-frame default is a multiple of 128 and loses
nothing. [`parkDough`](synthesis.md#dough-kt--parkdough) registers a sink with that engine and returns a [`ParkedDough`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-parkeddough) closing both.

Read those two against the thread rule above: the sink builds its engine in its own constructor, on
whichever thread called it, and then renders it from the audio thread, and neither the sink nor
[`parkDough`](synthesis.md#dough-kt--parkdough) has a caller in the tree. The realtime path that does run is [`PatSpatialRoom`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialroom)'s, which
builds each engine inside the thread that will render it, one engine per spatial source, since an
engine is built with a single orbit and cannot keep simultaneous sources apart on its own.

## DoughDsp.kt { #doughdsp-kt }

Native Kotlin ports of low-level DSP from dough, carrying dough's AGPL-3.0 terms.

Ported from dough.c (https://codeberg.org/uzu/dough), which is
licensed AGPL-3.0. These are line-by-line ports, so this file is a
derivative work and the licence travels with it.

Within dough.c, the Dattorro reverb ([`PlateReverb`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-platereverb) here) is itself
noted as adapted from el-visio's MIT-licensed implementation of the
algorithm in Jon Dattorro, "Effect Design Part 1: Reverberator and
Other Filters" (1997):
  https://ccrma.stanford.edu/~dattorro/EffectDesignPart1.pdf

This file complements the WASM binding in Dough.kt rather than competing
with it: that path runs the real dough engine and nothing here affects it.
What follows is the subset of dough's primitives that the rest of
afield.audio.synth does not cover.

- [`DoughMath`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-doughmath) — fast float approximations (log2/exp2/pow/sin)
- [`PlateReverb`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-platereverb) — Dattorro plate reverb, mono in, stereo out
- [`Phaser`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-phaser) — LFO-swept cascaded notches
- [`ChamberlinLowpass`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-chamberlinlowpass) — the "superdough" 2-pole lowpass and its resonance curve
- [`CurvedADSR`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-curvedadsr) — time-based ADSR with click-free retrigger
- [`SoftDistort`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-softdistort) — dough's expm1 k-curve soft clipper
- [`ZawOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-zawosc) and [`PulzeOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-pulzeosc) — naive saw and pulse, aliasing included

Skipped as already covered by this package: polyBLEP saw/pulse/square/
tri (Oscillators.kt, in double precision), white/pink/brown noise
(same coefficients), the Audio-EQ-Cookbook biquad (Filters.kt),
delay (Effects.kt), flanger/chorus (Effects.kt), bit crush + sample-rate
reduction (Effects.kt BitCrusher), and lag (Envelopes.kt Slew). The
voice allocator, event/mini-notation parser, orbits and scheduler are
out of scope — use the WASM engine for those.

The oscillators here live alongside the rest of the port rather than in
Oscillators.kt so that the licence attribution above covers one file.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/)

**Used in:** [DoughDSP: hear the primitives](../dough_dsp_sound.md)

### DoughMath { #doughdsp-kt-doughmath }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DoughMath</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/#L68)

dough's hand-rolled float math. Cheaper and less accurate than `kotlin.math`; the inaccuracy is audible and is part of the character of [`ChamberlinLowpass`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-chamberlinlowpass) and [`Phaser`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-phaser), which recompute coefficients with these on every sample.

class="nc">LiveGraphInspectable</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/#L204)

Jon Dattorro's plate reverb: a pre-delay and input-diffusion chain feeding a figure-of-eight tank of two cross-coupled halves, each with its own all-pass diffusers and damping lowpass. The stereo image comes from summing seven taps per side at points scattered through the tank, so it is decorrelated rather than merely panned — this is what makes it sound different from [`FreeVerb`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-freeverb) and [`SpringReverb`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-springreverb).

### Phaser { #doughdsp-kt-phaser }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Phaser</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">rate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mf">0.5f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">depth</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mf">0.5f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">center</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1000f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sweep</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">600f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mix</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">SignalProcessor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/#L464)

Two cascaded notch filters swept by a sine LFO, the second offset 282 Hz above the first. Detuning is exponential (in cents), so the sweep sounds even across the range, and [`depth`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt--phaser--depth) widens the notches by lowering their Q rather than by moving them further.

### ChamberlinLowpass { #doughdsp-kt-chamberlinlowpass }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">ChamberlinLowpass</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">cutoff</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1000f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">resonance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">0f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">SignalProcessor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/#L567)

Two-pole Chamberlin-style state-variable lowpass, in the exact form strudel/superdough uses. Distinct from [`SVF`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-svf) (trapezoidal, zero-delay feedback) in both topology and, more audibly, in the resonance curve: damping is `0.5^((resonance + 0.125) / 0.125)`, so the useful range is squeezed into the top of the [`resonance`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt--chamberlinlowpass--resonance) knob and it snarls rather than whistles as it approaches self-oscillation.

### SoftDistort { #doughdsp-kt-softdistort }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">SoftDistort</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">amount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">postGain</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Param</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Param</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="mi">1f</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">SignalProcessor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDsp/#L753)

The soft clipper from superdough: `y = (1+k)x / (1 + k|x|)` with `k = e^amount - 1`, so [`amount`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt--softdistort--amount) maps to drive exponentially and the output stays bounded by `(1+k)/k` however hard it is pushed.

## DoughDspSoundDocs.kt { #doughdspsounddocs-kt }

Headless **offline sound-render harness** for the dough DSP ports in `DoughDsp.kt`: every audible
example on the docs page is produced by running one of those primitives on the CPU.

Each scene in [`SCENES`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughdspsounddocs--scenes) renders a real graph. A pluck into [`PlateReverb`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-platereverb), a sawtooth through a
sweeping [`Phaser`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-phaser) or [`ChamberlinLowpass`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-chamberlinlowpass), an oscillator gated by [`CurvedADSR`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-curvedadsr), a sine driven
through [`SoftDistort`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-softdistort), raw [`ZawOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-zawosc) and [`PulzeOsc`](synthesis.md#doughdsp-kt-pulzeosc) tones: none of them is a synthesized or
hand-authored waveform. There is no realtime engine, no audio device, no GPU and no Field window.
Signals are block-rendered into a `FloatArray`, the same way [`DoughDspPlotGallery`](audio.md#doughdspplotgallery-kt-doughdspplotgallery) renders the
samples it plots, then written to a 16-bit PCM WAV through [`WavFloatArrayWriter`](audio.md#wavfloatarraywriter-kt-wavfloatarraywriter). The render is
deterministic, so a committed docs `.wav` regenerates byte-stably at docs-build.

This is the default renderer for the `audio="…"` docs-capture mode (see `public/docs_hooks.py`). A
fence can name a different one with `audio-renderer=`; `CaSoundDocs` and `FaustPolySoundDocs` are
two harnesses of this shape that other pages reach that way.

The public building blocks are the top-level `dough*` helpers below: [`doughRenderMono`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughrendermono),
[`doughRenderStereoMono`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughrenderstereomono), [`doughRenderGated`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughrendergated) and [`doughPluckEnv`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughpluckenv) to render, then
[`doughAbsEnvelope`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughabsenvelope), [`doughShortTimeRms`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughshorttimerms), [`doughShortTimeBrightness`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughshorttimebrightness) and [`doughWaveWindow`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughwavewindow) to shape
what is plotted. The docs page's runner blocks call those same functions, so the code a reader sees
building a primitive and plotting it is the code that ran, and the graph it builds is the graph the
`audio=` WAV was rendered from. `afield.audio.synth` is auto-imported into every box, so a docs
fence calls them unqualified.

As a FIELD_TEST (`synth.dough-dsp.sound`) it renders every scene to a temp dir and checks the
samples it got: a valid WAV header on disk whose declared sample rate and data size agree with the
bytes, and then per scene, that the reverb tail decays, that the ADSR rhythm has silent gaps, that
the filter sweep gets brighter, that the drive sweep adds harmonics, and that the raw oscillator is
periodic. It writes no committed assets while doing that.

Add a sound by appending one [`Scene`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughdspsounddocs--scene) to [`SCENES`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughdspsounddocs--scenes).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DoughDspSoundDocs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughDspSoundDocs/)

**Used in:** [DoughDSP: hear the primitives](../dough_dsp_sound.md)

## DoughLive.kt { #doughlive-kt }

Box-level dough: `sound("/dough/play/note/60/s/sine/...")` from any box, and `thisRMS`, the level
that box's own sounds are making right now.

The paths are dough's, unchanged, so a path copied from a browser demo running `dough.wasm` plays
the same here: [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) runs the same module. One [`DoughLive`](synthesis.md#doughlive-kt-doughlive) serves the whole process. It
builds its engine on its own render thread (a [`DoughEngine`](synthesis.md#dough-kt-doughengine) admits only the thread that built it)
and passes audio to [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) through a short [`PatSpatialRing`](patterns.md#patspatial-kt-patspatialring), so nothing dough does,
booting included, happens on the audio thread.

Every box gets a dough `group` number, and [`Box.sound`](synthesis.md#doughlive-kt--sound) tags the box's events with it. After every
block the render thread reads each sounding voice's group and output sample out of the module's
memory ([`DoughEngine.voiceFrames`](synthesis.md#dough-kt--doughengine--voiceframes)) and keeps a running mean square per group, so [`Box.thisRMS`](synthesis.md#doughlive-kt--thisrms) is
measured from what the box's voices actually produced, not estimated from the numbers in its paths.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/DoughLive.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/DoughLive/)

## Effects.kt { #effects-kt }

The mono effects: delays, reverbs, distortions and dynamics, each one a [`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor) that `/`
pipes a signal into.

`saw / Delay(0.25.p)` is the whole calling convention. Every control is a [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param) rendered once per
sample, so a delay time or a compressor threshold can itself be a signal, and a sweep of one lands
sample-accurate rather than once a block. All of them take and return mono; stereo comes after
them, from [`Pan`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-pan) or [`StereoSignal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereosignal).

The delay-line readers are not uniform, and it is audible. [`Delay`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-delay) interpolates between samples
with a cubic fit; [`Chorus`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-chorus) and [`Flanger`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-flanger) read the nearest whole sample, so a slow sweep through
either of those has a faint stepping to it that [`Delay`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-delay) does not. [`Compressor`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-compressor) and [`Limiter`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-limiter) also
keep a running trace of their own gain reduction, which is what the meters in `Visualizers.kt`
draw.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Effects.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Effects/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md)

## Envelopes.kt { #envelopes-kt }

Control shapes: [`Gate`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-gate), [`ADSR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-adsr), [`AR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-ar), [`Line`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-line) and [`BreakpointEnvelope`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-breakpointenvelope) generate one, [`Slew`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-slew) limits
how fast one can move, and [`EnvelopeFollower`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-envelopefollower) recovers one from a signal that already exists.

Everything here is a [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) rather than a [`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor), so `/` does not reach it. An
envelope is applied by multiplying, `SawOsc(220.p) * env`, and the two that read a signal take it
as a constructor argument instead of through an input. What comes out is a stream of samples like
any other, so an envelope can be handed to a filter cutoff or a delay time as readily as to an
amplitude.

Times are in seconds throughout, and the gated envelopes watch a signal rather than wait for a
method call: [`ADSR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-adsr) follows the level of its gate and holds at sustain while it is high, [`AR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-ar) fires
on the rising edge and runs to the end regardless. Every `curve` argument is an exponent applied to
a normalised ramp, so 1 is linear, below 1 starts fast and above 1 starts slow.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Envelopes.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Envelopes/)

**Used in:** [Visualizers, Displays, and Little Instruments](../visualizers.md)

## FM.kt { #fm-kt }

Frequency-modulation synthesis in two pieces: [`FMOperator`](synthesis.md#fm-kt-fmoperator) is one modulated sine, and [`FMPatch`](synthesis.md#fm-kt-fmpatch)
wires several of them into the classic algorithms.

An operator is phase modulation rather than true frequency modulation. Its phase advances at
`freq`, and the modulation is added to that phase where the sine is read rather than to the
frequency, so it does not accumulate. Operators are connected by assigning to `pmInput`, and since
the modulator is an ordinary [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) the modulation index is a gain in front of it:
`car.pmInput = mod * Param(3f)`. `feedbackAmount` adds an operator's own last sample to its phase,
and unlike the rest it is a plain `Float` fixed at construction rather than a [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param).

[`FMPatch`](synthesis.md#fm-kt-fmpatch) is three builders over that one part, each returning a bare [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) to be enveloped and
piped onward like any other source. `twoOp` is a modulator into a carrier at a frequency ratio,
`threeOp` is a three-operator serial chain, and `fourOp` takes an `algorithm` number choosing
between a serial chain, two modulators summed into one, two independent stacks mixed, and four
carriers added together. Any other number throws.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/FM.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/FM/)

## FaustBox.kt { #faustbox-kt }

The box-facing side of Faust: compile a program, play it, show what it declares.

`faust` is the call that matters. It strips the `#faust` marker, compiles, instantiates, and
returns a [`FaustLaunch`](synthesis.md#faustbox-kt-faustlaunch):

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
faust("""
#faust
import("stdfaust.lib");
freq = hslider("freq [unit:Hz]", 220, 50, 1000, 0.01);
process = os.sawtooth(freq) : fi.lowpass(2, 1200) * 0.2 <: _,_;
""")
```

Returning that launch as the box's last expression is what ties the sound to the box: it stays lit
while the program runs, and stopping the box stops the sound and closes the DSP's GraalVM context.
`registerFaustLaunchReturnValue` is the handler that does both. It exists because the generic audio
handler would close the audio patch and leave the context alive, which is one leaked context per
box run.

Everything else is a separate call, so a box shows only what it wants to:

 * `faustControls` turns the program's own `hslider`, `button` and `hgroup` declarations into a
   Field control group. Nobody writes the sliders, and a control group is what the phone's Group
   page publishes, so they are reachable from a phone at no extra cost.
 * `faustDiagram` displays Faust's own SVG block diagram of the program.
 * `faustWaveform` renders a program offline and plots it. Nothing there touches the audio engine,
   so it works where there is no audio device at all.
 * `faustCompile` compiles without playing, for looking at a program's interface or its diagram.

Every line number the compiler reports is shifted back onto the box's own lines before a marker is
placed, because the `#faust` line and any blank lines above it are not part of what the compiler
saw. [`stripFaustHeader`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt--stripfaustheader) removes them and reports how many lines went.

## FaustDsp.kt { #faustdsp-kt }

One compiled Faust program, instantiated and ready to make sound.

A [`FaustProgram`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt-faustprogram) is bytes; [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp) is the running thing. It holds its own WebAssembly instance
in its own GraalVM context, and `render` pulls audio out of it a block at a time, which is exactly
the shape [`StereoRenderable`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereorenderable) wants: a Faust program sits in Field's audio graph next to an
oscillator with no adaptation. [`FaustNode`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustnode) is what puts it there.

### It is fast, and the cost is the boundary rather than the DSP

Measured for a sawtooth-through-a-filter voice at 48kHz, where a 128-frame block has 2667µs to
render in:

 * `compute` on its own: **7.6µs**, about 350 times realtime. Generated Faust is not the
   bottleneck.
 * `render`, end to end through [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp): **60.4µs**.

The gap is the JVM↔WebAssembly boundary, and two things keep it as small as that: the output is
copied with one bulk `Value.readBuffer` per channel rather than a sample at a time, and the JS
entry points are resolved once at construction rather than per block. What is left is dominated by
the per-block `Context.enter`, which is where to look next if it ever matters. The figures above
are one machine's; what `synth.faust.smoke` holds to is a floor of ten times realtime.

The compiler, by contrast, *is* slow: see [`FaustEngine`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt-faustengine), which keeps it behind a separate context
for that reason.

### The context is single-threaded, so parameters are queued

A GraalVM context cannot be entered by two threads at once, and `render` runs on the audio thread.
So `setParam` does not touch WebAssembly at all: it enqueues, and `render` drains the queue before
computing. That is also the right audio-engineering answer, with no lock on the audio thread and no
parameter changing halfway through a block.

A queue rather than a last-write-wins map, because a `button` is momentary: collapsing a
press and its release into one value would silently swallow a note.

## FaustEditorExtension.kt { #fausteditorextension-kt }

The `#faust` editor extension and the vocabulary it completes against.

Both are static resources rather than strings built here. `faust.js` is served to the browser as
the AMD module `bithero/faust`, which `bootstrapMonaco.js` lists alongside the other language
extensions, and it fetches `faust-vocabulary.json` itself at install time. This object reads the
two files verbatim, so the node probe in `FaustEditorExtensionWorkout` exercises the code and
data that ship rather than a copy of them.

The vocabulary is extracted by `tools/generate_faust_vocabulary.py` from Faust's standard
libraries, which are not on disk: they ship packed inside the vendored compiler's
`libfaust-wasm.data`. Completion therefore offers the thousand-odd functions that the same
vendored compiler will resolve `import("stdfaust.lib")` against, with their real signatures.

## FaustEngine.kt { #faustengine-kt }

The Faust compiler, running inside Field.

[Faust](https://faust.grame.fr) is a functional language for signal processing that compiles to
efficient code. Field embeds the compiler itself as WebAssembly, in
`src/jvmMain/resources/faust/` with a `PROVENANCE.md` beside it, and runs it in the same GraalVM
runtime that already hosts `dough.wasm`. There is nothing to install on any platform: the build
that loads is the one committed in the repository, and `synth.faust.smoke` asserts its version
against `EXPECTED_LIBFAUST_VERSION`.

### Two halves, opposite performance

Measured on an aarch64 Mac under GraalVM CE 25.0.2, and the reason the object is shaped the way it
is:

 * **Generated DSP is fast.** `compute` on a compiled program takes ~7.6µs of the 2667µs a
   128-frame block has at 48kHz; end to end through [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp) it is ~60µs, and what separates
   those two figures is the JVM↔WebAssembly boundary rather than Faust. `synth.faust.smoke`
   asserts a floor of ten times realtime, so playing is not a performance problem here.
 * **The compiler is slow.** `compile` settles at ~600ms once Truffle has warmed, against ~30ms
   for the same call under Node's V8, and the *first* compile of a process pays 13–22s of warm-up.

Three things follow:

 1. The compiler gets **its own GraalVM context**, never shared with a [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp). A 600ms compile
    holding a lock the audio thread wants every 2.67ms would be audible as a dropout.
 2. `warmInBackground` pays the 13–22s while Field is starting, rather than at the moment someone
    first runs a box.
 3. `compile` is memoised on the hash of (source, arguments), so re-running an unchanged box, or
    undoing back to a program already seen, costs nothing.

### Errors

The vendored compiler is an Emscripten build with exception catching disabled, so *every* failure
arrives as an opaque `"Exception catching is disabled"` RuntimeError. The real message is only
available afterwards, from `getErrorAfterException()`, and it is well formed:
`"probe:2 : ERROR : undefined symbol : sawtoothX"`. [`FaustCompileError`](synthesis.md#faustengine-kt-faustcompileerror) parses that into something
an editor marker can use.

## FaustPattern.kt { #faustpattern-kt }

A pattern plays a Faust program.

The join between two things that each need nothing added to them. Field's pattern language,
mini-notation over the `Pat` algebra in rational cycle time, says *when* and *what pitch*. A
compiled Faust program is one always-on DSP with sliders. This file is small because neither side
is modified and nothing is recompiled.

The whole conversion is one function, [`faustNotesForArc`](synthesis.md#faustpattern-kt--faustnotesforarc): a pattern event's rational arc becomes an integer
frame on the bank's own clock, and its atom becomes a frequency in Hz. Everything after that is integers,
which is why the timing can be asserted in samples.

## FaustPoly.kt { #faustpoly-kt }

A Faust program played polyphonically, by a pattern.

[`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp) is one instance of one program: a drone with knobs. This is the other thing a Faust program
can be, an *instrument*: N copies of the same compiled DSP allocated to notes, with the notes coming
from Field's own pattern language. Nothing in Faust is recompiled to make that happen. A Faust factory
built with internal memory keeps its whole state at offset 0 of its own WebAssembly memory, so N
`WebAssembly.Instance`s of one module are N independent voices for free.

### One context, N instances

Each [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp) builds its own GraalVM context, and what is left of a block after `compute` is dominated
by the per-block `Context.enter` (see [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp) for the figures). N voices as N [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp)s would pay
that entry N times a block, which would make the cost of polyphony a boundary cost rather than a DSP
cost. [`FaustVoiceBank`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustvoicebank) hosts every voice in **one** context instead, one `enter` a block whatever N is.
That needs a host shim of its own: [`FaustDsp`](synthesis.md#faustdsp-kt-faustdsp)'s keeps its instance in module-level JS globals and can
hold only one.

Both arrangements are timed against each other by `synth.faust.poly`, which prints the µs-per-block
curve for each and asserts that the one shipped here renders a block inside the block's own budget at
1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 voices.

### The notes land on the sample, not on the block

A 128-frame block at 48kHz is 2.67ms, and quantising a note onset to that boundary is audible. So
`render` does not write parameters once per block. It enters the context once, then walks the block in
**chunks that end where the next event begins**: apply the writes due at this exact frame, `compute` up
to the next event, repeat. A note therefore begins on the sample it was scheduled for, and
`synth.faust.poly` asserts that in samples rather than in milliseconds.

This is also why `FaustDsp.setParam` is not used: that queue is drained once per `render` call, which is
block granularity by construction.

### The controls are the program's own, and it says so when they are missing

Faust's polyphonic convention is `freq` / `gate` / `gain`, the same three names its `-nvoices`
architecture looks for, and they are discovered out of the program's declared UI by label rather than by
index. `gain` is optional; a program missing `freq` or `gate` is refused by [`FaustPolyControls`](synthesis.md#faustpoly-kt-faustpolycontrols), with a
message naming what is missing, what the program *did* declare, and the line of Faust that would fix it.
Writing to control index 0 instead would produce silence, which carries no diagnosis at all.

## FieldAudioEngine.kt { #fieldaudioengine-kt }

The file that opens an audio device: the OpenAL output stream Field plays through, the optional
capture stream `audioInput()` reads from, and the mixer that sums every registered patch into it.

[`AudioPatchSpec`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-audiopatchspec) is one thing to hear, either a mono [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) with a gain and a pan or a
[`StereoRenderable`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereorenderable) with a gain. A box builds one by returning `audio { … }` from `synth.kt` rather
than by calling the constructors here. [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) is the device and the list of patches on
it; `shared()`, reached from a box as `audioEngine()`, is the single instance a process gets, and
its sample rate and buffer size are whatever the first caller in the session asked for. `register`
takes a spec and hands back an [`AudioPatchHandle`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-audiopatchhandle), and closing that handle is the only way a patch
leaves the mix.

Rendering is pulled by the device rather than driven by a clock. One daemon thread keeps a queue of
OpenAL buffers filled, `bufferSize` frames each, and renders the next block only when the source
reports an earlier buffer as processed, so the mix advances as fast as the sound card consumes it
and no faster. A [`SynthContext`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-synthcontext) is advanced once per block and handed to every patch. Patches
accumulate rather than replace: each renderer adds into the same pair of buffers, a mono one
through an equal-power pan law that puts a centred signal at 0.707 in both channels rather than at
half in each. The sum is clamped to [-1, 1] and written out as 16-bit stereo, and a sample that is
not finite becomes silence and is counted in `nonFiniteSamplesSanitized`, which reaches the
`warning,audio` log channel at most once every two seconds.

Three properties of that loop account for most silence. `outputActive` means the device opened, not
that audio is flowing: it is set when the OpenAL source and its buffers exist and cleared only when
the thread exits, while rendering depends on that source continuing to report processed buffers. A
machine too loaded to service its own audio daemon therefore renders nothing with every flag still
reading true, and a patch that counts its own `generateStereo` calls is what separates that case
from a wiring mistake. If the device cannot be opened at all, the thread prints why and returns
without retrying, so `start()` does nothing from then on and patches register into a mix nobody
renders; `destroyShared()` forces a fresh attempt. And input is the newest block the capture device
has rather than a continuous stream: at most `bufferSize` frames are taken per block, and a block
with nothing ready reads as silence.

`enableLinkOutput` sends the same mix on to Ableton Link through [`LinkAudioInterface`](audio.md#abletonlinkaudio-kt-linkaudiointerface), and can mute
the local device while it does by zeroing the OpenAL source gain; the mix is rendered either way. A
Link interface opened anywhere else in the process is picked up per block without this file being
told about it, so a patch can reach Link without the call.

## Filters.kt { #filters-kt }

The filters, and the one saturator that keeps them company. Each is a [`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor), so
`saw / SVF(cutoff = 800.p)` is how one gets used, and every coefficient is recomputed per sample
from its [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param)s, which is what lets a cutoff be swept at audio rate.

Which one to reach for. [`SVF`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-svf) is the default for anything modulated: it is the state-variable form
under a topology-preserving transform, and it stays well behaved while the cutoff is moving.
[`Biquad`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-biquad) is the Audio EQ Cookbook set, second order in eight responses including the two shelves
and a peaking EQ, and is what to use for a fixed curve. [`OnePole`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-onepole) is 6 dB per octave and costs
almost nothing. [`MoogLadder`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-moogladder) and [`DiodeLadder`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-diodeladder) are four-pole resonant lowpasses that keep the
character of the circuits they are named after.

The rest are more particular. [`CombFilter`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-combfilter) and [`AllpassFilter`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-allpassfilter) are the classic reverb building
blocks offered raw, in feedforward or feedback form; the reverbs in `Effects.kt` build their own
rather than compose these. [`FormantFilter`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-formantfilter) parks three bandpasses on vowel formants and morphs
between A, E, I, O and U on a single control. [`DCBlocker`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-dcblocker) is the one-line high-pass that removes
the offset rectification and asymmetric shaping leave behind. [`Saturator`](synthesis.md#filters-kt-saturator) is a bare `tanh` with a
drive in front of it, which is often what a ladder filter's output wants next.

## FnSignal.kt { #fnsignal-kt }

Plays a [`Functions.Fn`](math.md#functions-kt--functions--fn) of time as audio, evaluating it at every sample rather than once per block.

[`FnSignal`](synthesis.md#fnsignal-kt-fnsignal) wraps the function and [`toSignal`](synthesis.md#fnsignal-kt--tosignal) is the extension that builds one, so an envelope or
frequency contour written as an `Fn` can drive a synth graph sample-accurately.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/FnSignal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/FnSignal/)

**Used in:** [A function, played and read back](../chain_fn_sound_roundtrip.md)

## FnSoundDocs.kt { #fnsounddocs-kt }

One `Functions.Fn` taken through sound and back, and the distance between what went in and what
came out — the harness behind `public/docs/chain_fn_sound_roundtrip.md`.

The route is four parts of Field that do not know about each other. [`contour`](synthesis.md#fnsounddocs-kt--fnsounddocs--contour) is built from
formula ops only, so `afield.math.functions.FnInterval` can certify its range on any interval. It enters a
Dough graph either per sample, through [`FnSignal`](synthesis.md#fnsignal-kt-fnsignal), or per block, through `Param { … }`. The graph is
rendered offline by [`doughRenderMono`](synthesis.md#doughdspsounddocs-kt--doughrendermono), written to a 16-bit WAV **without normalisation** — so the
amplitude in the file is the amplitude the function asked for — and read back from that file. The
analysis is the in-process pair `PatOnsetDetection` and `PatPitchDetection` already provide: an RMS
envelope ([`patEnergyEnvelope`](patterns.md#patonsetdetection-kt--patenergyenvelope)) for loudness, and YIN ([`patF0Frames`](patterns.md#patpitchdetection-kt--patf0frames)) for pitch.

### Two encodings of one function

* `Encoding.LOUDNESS`: a [`CARRIER_HZ`](synthesis.md#fnsounddocs-kt--fnsounddocs--carrier-hz) sine whose amplitude is `LOUDNESS_GAIN · f(t)`. Recovered as
  `√2 · RMS / LOUDNESS_GAIN`. The carrier is chosen so one period is exactly 128 samples at
  [`SR`](synthesis.md#fnsounddocs-kt--fnsounddocs--sr) and the RMS window, [`RMS_WINDOW`](synthesis.md#fnsounddocs-kt--fnsounddocs--rms-window), holds two whole periods: then a steady sine's RMS is
  exactly `A/√2` and the window adds no ripple of its own.
* `Encoding.PITCH`: a sine at `PITCH_BASE_HZ · 2^f(t)` and constant level, so `f` spans a fraction of
  an octave. Recovered as `log2(hz / PITCH_BASE_HZ)` from voiced YIN frames only.

### What is measured, per encoding and route

Every analysis frame is one sample of the population: its recovered value against `f` at the frame
centre (`RoundTrip.maxAbsError`, `RoundTrip.rmsError`); the delay that best aligns them
(`RoundTrip.bestLagSamples`); and whether the recovered value lies inside the **certified** range of
`f` over the samples the frame actually read (`RoundTrip.insideCertified`) — the only interval a
windowed measurement can be expected to land in. [`Blip`](synthesis.md#fnsounddocs-kt--fnsounddocs--blip) is the narrow feature: a bump
with a 3 ms sigma, shorter than both analysis windows, and how much of its height comes back.

No engine, no device, no Field window. The renders are deterministic, so the committed `.wav`s
regenerate byte-stably; as a FIELD_TEST everything is written to a temp dir.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/FnSoundDocs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/FnSoundDocs/)

## HarmonicPhaseTracker.kt { #harmonicphasetracker-kt }

Pitch and phase tracking for harmonically rich monophonic input, through [`HarmonicPhaseTracker`](synthesis.md#harmonicphasetracker-kt-harmonicphasetracker).

A bank of complex harmonic demodulators votes on the fundamental's phase velocity, and a
decimated autocorrelation search reacquires the period when the bank falls into an octave trap.
The tracker is a [`PhaseTracker`](synthesis.md#trackedphase-kt-phasetracker), so its state can drive a [`TrackedPhaseBank`](synthesis.md#trackedphasebank-kt-trackedphasebank).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/HarmonicPhaseTracker.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/HarmonicPhaseTracker/)

## LaunchBundle.kt { #launchbundle-kt }

`+` for the audio return values, so one box can launch more than one thing.

A box launches whatever its last expression evaluates to, and `ReturnValueRegistry` reads a
`LaunchBundle`, or any `Iterable`, as a request to launch every item in it. `afield` supplies the
`+` that builds a bundle from a `Frames` or from a bundle already in hand; this file supplies it
for the three audio types a box is likely to be holding on the left, so
`audio { SineOsc(220.0) } + pat("bd sd").respond { … }` is one box playing a drone and a pattern.

A chain of `+` produces one flat list rather than a nest: the bundle flattens what it already has
each time it grows, and the registry flattens again before it dispatches. Each item then goes
through the same handler chain it would have reached on its own, the box reads as running until
the last of them stops, and an item no handler recognises is logged on the `warn,execution`
channel rather than dropped in silence.

## Oscillators.kt { #oscillators-kt }

The sources: oscillators, noise, and the samplers that stand in for one. All of them are [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal)s
taking [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param)s, so a frequency can itself be an oscillator and FM costs nothing to ask for.

[`SawOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-sawosc), [`SquareOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-squareosc), [`PulseOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-pulseosc) and [`TriOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-triosc) are corrected with PolyBLEP, a polynomial stand-in
for a bandlimited step subtracted at each discontinuity, so they hold up at the top of the keyboard
where a naive ramp would fold. [`SineOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-sineosc) has nothing to correct, and [`Phasor`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-phasor)'s bare 0-to-1 ramp is
the phase source to start from when shaping a waveform of your own.

[`SuperSaw`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-supersaw) is a detuned bank with the spread, the blend, the detune curve and the phase alignment
all exposed. The `Super*` voices beside it are continuous ports of the SuperDirt synths of the same
names, so a pattern written for Tidal has something to play. [`WavetableOsc`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-wavetableosc) reads a single cycle out
of a `FloatArray`, and [`Wavetables`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-wavetables) builds the ordinary ones by summing harmonics.

The three noise generators differ in spectrum: [`WhiteNoise`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-whitenoise) is flat, [`PinkNoise`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-pinknoise) is a bank of
one-pole filters over white and falls about 3 dB per octave, [`BrownNoise`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-brownnoise) is a leaky random walk and
falls about 6. [`Impulse`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-impulse) emits one sample of 1 each time its phase wraps, which is the trigger
[`SampleAndHold`](synthesis.md#oscillators-kt-sampleandhold) is usually waiting for.

`synth.kt` carries lowercase aliases for the common ones (`sine`, `saw`, `white`), and each one
hands back a fresh instance every time it is read.

## ParamQuery.kt { #paramquery-kt }

The synth-facing head of the graph-query layer: turn a [`PathSet`](data.md#graphquery-kt-pathset) into a set of *drivable
parameters*.

Two kinds of slot qualify, behind one `ParamBinding` interface:

 - a native [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param) (base + supplier + modulation), grouped by identity so several
   addresses for one Param collapse into a single entry with `aliases`;
 - any writable numeric property, wrapped in a `ScalarPathState` that gives a plain
   `Int`/`Float`/`Double`/… field the same base/supplier/modulation semantics, coercing
   back to the field's declared type on write.

That second case is what makes *any* object's numeric field modulatable,
which is why the generic query core underneath knows nothing
about audio.

The split runs along the same line. Path resolution, grouping and `ScalarPathState` carry no
runloop dependency, and this file is where the runloop-bound half of the param layer is confined.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/ParamQuery.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/ParamQuery/)

## PdBox.kt { #pdbox-kt }

The box-facing side of Pure Data: a patch as a sound source, with messages both ways.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val patch = pd("""
#X obj 20 20 r freq;
#X obj 20 60 osc~ 220;
#X obj 20 100 *~ 0.1;
#X obj 20 140 dac~;
#X connect 0 0 1 0;
#X connect 1 0 2 0;
#X connect 2 0 3 0;
#X connect 2 0 3 1;
""")
controlGroup { slider("freq", 100.0, 1000.0, initialValue = 220.0) { patch.send("freq", it) } }
patch
```

Returning the [`PdLaunch`](synthesis.md#pdbox-kt-pdlaunch) as the box's last expression is what makes it sound: it joins
[`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine) as a [`afield.audio.pd.PdNode`](synthesis.md#pdinstance-kt-pdnode) — the same seam Faust and `patSynth` use — and stopping
the box stops the sound and frees the Pd. Everything Pd prints (``print``, errors) goes to the
box's output, and an object Pd could not create is marked on the box's own line.

Every launch is its own Pd, so two boxes can both use `[r freq]` without hearing each other.
libpd is an optional native library; see [`PdLibrary`](synthesis.md#pdnative-kt-pdlibrary).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/PdBox.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/PdBox/)

**Used in:** [Pure Data](../pure_data.md), [Agent transcript gallery](../agent_transcripts.md)

## Physical.kt { #physical-kt }

Two processors over one delay line read at fractional sample positions: [`FractionalDelay`](synthesis.md#physical-kt-fractionaldelay), a plain
echo, and [`KarplusStrong`](synthesis.md#physical-kt-karplusstrong), the same line closed into a loop and tuned to a pitch.

[`DelayInterpolation`](synthesis.md#physical-kt-delayinterpolation) picks how the line reads between whole samples. `LINEAR` mixes the two
neighbours, `CUBIC`, the default, fits four of them. The choice matters most inside a feedback
loop, where the read happens again on every pass.

[`FractionalDelay`](synthesis.md#physical-kt-fractionaldelay) is the echo: `delayTime` in seconds against a line sized from `maxDelaySec` and
the sample rate it first sees, `feedback` clamped just inside ±1 so each pass is quieter than the
last, and `mix` crossfading dry against delayed. [`Delay`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-delay) in `Effects.kt` does the same job with a
fixed cubic read; this one lets the interpolation be chosen.

[`KarplusStrong`](synthesis.md#physical-kt-karplusstrong) closes that line into a loop one period of `freq` long. Two things happen inside
it. `brightness` crossfades the delayed sample against the one before it, an average of two taps
that acts as a lowpass, so the high harmonics fade a pass at a time while the low ones hold, and
the loop length has that average's own delay subtracted from it, which keeps the pitch where it
was as `brightness` moves. `decay` scales the whole of what goes back round on each pass.

The excitation reaches the loop through a second line, delayed by `pickPosition` of a period and
subtracted from itself before `excitationMix` scales it in. That is a comb with notches every
`1 / pickPosition` harmonics, which is the standard stand-in for where along a string it was
plucked, so moving the control changes the colour of the attack rather than its level. It is a
[`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor), so `burst / KarplusStrong(freq = 110.p)` is how it gets used, and with
`clearOnTrigger` a rising edge on `trigger` empties both lines so a new note starts clean.

## Sampling.kt { #sampling-kt }

Playback of recorded audio, from reading a buffer straight through to scattering it into grains.
[`AudioSample`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-audiosample) is the buffer, [`Sampler`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-sampler) plays one back, and the three grain clouds take one apart.

Every read goes through a four-point Hermite fit that wraps at both ends of the buffer rather than
clamping, so a position past the last sample continues from the first. [`Sampler`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-sampler) starts on the
rising edge of its `gate` and either runs to the end or loops between `loopStart` and `loopEnd`;
it scales its read rate by the ratio of the sample's own rate to the engine's, so a recording made
at 48 kHz plays at pitch on a 44.1 kHz output.

The three clouds spawn grains the same way and differ in where the grains read from. [`GrainCloud`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-graincloud)
reads a fixed [`AudioSample`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-audiosample) and sums to mono. [`StereoGrainCloud`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-stereograincloud) reads the same kind of sample but
gives each grain a pan position, a left/right read-head separation and independent per-channel
scatter, so it is a [`StereoNode`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereonode) rather than a [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal). [`LiveGrainCloud`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-livegraincloud) has no sample at all and
grains a ring buffer that its own input is writing.

Spawning is by accumulated density rather than by a clock: `density` is grains per second,
`densityJitter` varies the gap between onsets, and each cloud holds `maxGrains` voices, 128 by
default. A spawn that finds every voice busy is dropped rather than stealing one, so pushing
`density` past what `maxGrains` can carry thins the texture instead of cutting grains short.
`spray`, `pitchJitterCents`, `grainSizeJitter` and `gainJitter` each widen one property per grain
at spawn time, [`GrainDirection`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-graindirection) decides whether a grain reads forwards, backwards or picks one per
grain, and [`GrainEnvelope`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-grainenvelope) is the window over a grain's life, eight shapes, with `randomEnvelope`
drawing a fresh one each time.

[`LiveGrainCloud`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-livegraincloud) also has to stay out of the recorder's way. A forward-reading grain is placed at
least its own travel distance back from the write head, as far as the ring allows, so it does not
overtake the recorder while it sounds. Its `record` control is a slewed gain on the write rather
than a switch, and at zero the write head stops advancing, so the grains go on working over
whatever the ring was holding.

## Signal.kt { #signal-kt }

The value types the rest of the synthesis category is written in, and the per-block contract they
render under. [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) is a mono source rendered a block at a time; [`Param`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-param) is a control value that
is itself a [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal), so anything with a knob can be driven by anything that makes samples;
[`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor) is a [`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) that reads another one; [`StereoRenderable`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereorenderable) and [`StereoNode`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereonode) are the
two-channel half.

[`SynthContext`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-synthcontext) is what a block of rendering is handed: the sample rate and buffer size, how long
the graph has been running, the Ableton Link reading taken at the top of the block, and a
scratch-buffer pool to borrow from instead of allocating. Its `cycleId` is also the cache key that
makes sharing safe, since [`Signal.render`](synthesis.md#signal-kt--signal--render) evaluates a node once per block and replays the result to
every later reader. That is why `val o = sine; o + o * 0.5f` is one oscillator heard twice rather
than two that have drifted apart.

Arithmetic on signals builds graph nodes rather than numbers, and `/` is overloaded twice: a
[`Signal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signal) on the right divides sample by sample, a [`SignalProcessor`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-signalprocessor) on the right pipes into it.
Most of the nodes those operators construct are private. [`Const`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-const), [`Mix`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-mix), [`Pan`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-pan) and [`StereoSignal`](synthesis.md#signal-kt-stereosignal)
are public, for graphs you would rather assemble by hand.

Nothing here opens an audio device. Closing a graph with `audio { … }` and returning it from a box
is what reaches [`FieldAudioEngine`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-fieldaudioengine); `synth.kt` is the terse surface that does it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Signal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Signal/)

**Used in:** [How to make sound in Field](../sound_paths.md), [Faust](../faust.md), [A pattern that moves particles](../chain_pattern_particles.md)

## Spectral.kt { #spectral-kt }

The frequency-domain end of the synth: an [`FFT`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-fft), two short-time transforms built on it, and a
wavetable that keeps its waveforms as spectra.

[`FFT`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-fft) is radix-2 and in place, over interleaved `[re, im, re, im, …]` buffers whose length is a
power of two. It is not a shared service: [`PhaseVocoder`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-phasevocoder), [`SpectralFilter`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralfilter) and [`SpectralWavetable`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralwavetable)
each construct one at the size they work at.

[`PhaseVocoder`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-phasevocoder) and [`SpectralFilter`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralfilter) have the same shape. A Hann window is applied on the way in
and again on the way out, frames advance by `fftSize / hopFactor` samples, and the results are
overlap-added into a ring that is then drained one sample per output frame. `hopFactor` is 4 by
default, so four windows cover every sample. What they do in between differs. [`PhaseVocoder`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-phasevocoder) reads
an [`AudioSample`](synthesis.md#sampling-kt-audiosample), and its two controls act on different quantities: `timeStretch` scales how far
the analysis frame advances between hops while the output hop stays fixed, and `pitchShift` scales
each bin's phase advance, so neither one implies the other. [`SpectralFilter`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralfilter) reads its input and
multiplies each bin by whatever gain the caller's `transferFunction` returns for that bin's centre
frequency, mirroring the gain onto the negative-frequency half.

[`SpectralWavetable`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralwavetable) puts the same transform to a different use. It holds a fixed number of
single-cycle frames, eight of 2048 samples by default, and keeps each one as both a waveform and
its spectrum. Morphing between two frames interpolates the spectra rather than the waveforms, and
band-limiting is then a matter of zeroing every bin above a harmonic limit before transforming
back, so one table plays at any pitch with the harmonics that would fold removed. Writes and the
frame copy that starts a morph both take a lock, so a box thread can rewrite a frame while the
audio thread is playing the table.

[`SpectralWavetableRecorder`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralwavetablerecorder) and [`SpectralWavetableOsc`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralwavetableosc) are the two ends of that. The recorder
passes its input through untouched and, `captureRate` times a second, blends the most recent
`frameSize` samples of it into the one or two frames bracketing `position`, unless `freeze` is
positive. The oscillator takes its harmonic limit from the frequency it is playing and the
`brightness` control, renders the morphed waveform once per segment of `segmentSize` samples, and
crossfades across the segment when `position` moved during it. A table also remembers the position
the oscillator last asked for, and that is the position `Visualizers.kt` draws when a table is
displayed in a box.

## Subharmonic.kt { #subharmonic-kt }

Subharmonic synthesis: follow the pitch of a roughly monophonic input and generate a new tone
at a fraction of it — an octave down at `division = 2.0`, an octave and a fifth at `3.0`, a
fifth at `1.5`.

Three trackers share one output stage ([`SubharmonicTracker`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmonictracker)):

 * [`SubharmonicZeroCross`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmoniczerocross) times the gap between positive-going zero crossings. Cheap and
   instant, and it believes every crossing, so harmonics and noise that add crossings make it
   jump.
 * [`SubharmonicPLL`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmonicpll) is a second-order phase-locked loop with a multiplying phase detector. It
   owns a continuous phase and frequency estimate, so the output glides instead of jumping,
   but its error signal scales with the input's level and carries a ripple at twice the input
   frequency.
 * [`SubharmonicQuadPLL`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmonicquadpll) first splits the input into a quadrature pair with [`HilbertPair`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-hilbertpair), so it
   can measure the phase error directly — independent of level and free of that ripple — and
   adds a frequency discriminator that pulls the loop onto a new note quickly.

None of them divides the input's wrapped phase (`sin(phase / 2)` jumps by half a cycle every
time the phase wraps). Each keeps its own oscillator advancing at the tracked rate divided by
[`SubharmonicTracker.division`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt--subharmonictracker--division), so `division` can be any number, changed every sample.

A tracker is a per-sample object: call [`SubharmonicTracker.process`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt--subharmonictracker--process) on each sample, or put it in
a signal graph with [`Subharmonic`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmonic). It returns the generated subharmonic only; mix the input back
in yourself.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/Subharmonic.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Subharmonic/)

**Used in:** [Subharmonic Synthesis: an Octave Below](../subharmonic_sound.md)

### HilbertPair { #subharmonic-kt-hilbertpair }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">HilbertPair</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/Subharmonic/#L232)

A pair of allpass chains whose outputs stay 90° apart: [`i`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt--hilbertpair--i) and [`q`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt--hilbertpair--q) are the in-phase and quadrature parts of the analytic signal, so `atan2(i, q)` is the input's instantaneous phase and `hypot(i, q)` its instantaneous amplitude.

## SubharmonicSoundDocs.kt { #subharmonicsounddocs-kt }

Offline renders for the subharmonic page (`public/docs/subharmonic_sound.md`): every clip on it
is one of the trackers in `Subharmonic.kt` run on a real input — a Kotlin bassline, Dirt-Samples
one-shots from the pinned subset, or fourteen seconds of *Night of the Living Dead* (1968, public
domain) committed beside the page.

The page's runner blocks build the same graphs and plot them with [`subRender`](synthesis.md#subharmonicsounddocs-kt--subrender); each scene here
renders that graph again to a 16-bit WAV for the page's `audio=` fences. As a FIELD_TEST it renders
every scene and checks the claim the page makes about it: that the quadrature PLL lands within a
few hertz of each bass note, that the zero-crossing tracker jumps around on unfiltered speech and
stops when the speech is lowpassed, and so on.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/SubharmonicSoundDocs.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/SubharmonicSoundDocs/)

**Used in:** [Subharmonic Synthesis: an Octave Below](../subharmonic_sound.md)

## TrackedPhase.kt { #trackedphase-kt }

Pitch-tracked phase for voice banks: a tracker reduces one periodic sound to phase, phase
advance, pitch, level and confidence, and a bank gives every voice its own phase accumulator.

Each voice advances by

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
theta += ratio * (omega + lock * (phaseAdvance - omega))
```

This supports undertones, harmonics and irrational ratios without dividing wrapped phase.
`lock = 0` follows stable pitch; `lock = 1` also follows the tracker's phase corrections. It does
not force a voice onto an absolute input phase, so changing a ratio preserves continuity.

QuadPhaseTracker is the analysis half of SubharmonicQuadPLL, sharing its HilbertPair and
algorithm; [`Subharmonic`](synthesis.md#subharmonic-kt-subharmonic) keeps its own oscillator and level behaviour.
HarmonicPhaseTracker supplies the same state from several partials, including a missing
fundamental. Neither tracker separates polyphonic sources.

Trackers, states and voices belong to the audio thread. TrackedPhaseAnalysis caches each
sample's state for graph fan-out; reading a live tracker from the Runloop must never advance
it. Per-sample paths reuse their storage. Custom renderers must handle their own bandwidth;
the bank's Nyquist fade protects the fundamental of each sine voice only.

## TrackedPhaseBank.kt { #trackedphasebank-kt }

An oscillator bank that follows a tracked phase: [`TrackedPhaseBank`](synthesis.md#trackedphasebank-kt-trackedphasebank) renders a list of
[`PhaseVoice`](synthesis.md#trackedphasebank-kt-phasevoice)s, each advancing at a ratio of the pitch a [`PhaseTracker`](synthesis.md#trackedphase-kt-phasetracker) reports.

Each voice keeps its own continuous phase accumulator, so fractional and irrational ratios stay
continuous, and a [`PhaseRenderer`](synthesis.md#trackedphasebank-kt-phaserenderer) turns that phase into a sample (a sine by default).

## TrackedPhaseSignal.kt { #trackedphasesignal-kt }

Shares one phase-tracking analysis of a signal between several tracked-phase banks in a graph.

[`TrackedPhaseAnalysis`](synthesis.md#trackedphasesignal-kt-trackedphaseanalysis) runs its [`PhaseTracker`](synthesis.md#trackedphase-kt-phasetracker) over the source once per block and keeps the
per-sample states; each [`TrackedPhaseAnalysis.synthesize`](synthesis.md#trackedphasesignal-kt--trackedphaseanalysis--synthesize) call renders a [`TrackedPhaseBank`](synthesis.md#trackedphasebank-kt-trackedphasebank) from
those states, so the tracker advances once however many outputs read it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/audio/synth/TrackedPhaseSignal.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/TrackedPhaseSignal/)

### TrackedPhaseAnalysis { #trackedphasesignal-kt-trackedphaseanalysis }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">TrackedPhaseAnalysis</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">source</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Signal</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tracker</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">PhaseTracker</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">QuadPhaseTracker</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Signal</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/synth/TrackedPhaseSignal/#L20)

Analyze `source` once per graph block, retaining a reusable state for each sample. Several [`synthesize`](synthesis.md#trackedphasesignal-kt--trackedphaseanalysis--synthesize) outputs can share this analysis in one graph without advancing its tracker twice. Like other stateful signals, this belongs to one audio context; inspect published values rather than rendering the graph from a UI loop. Rendering this node itself returns the analysis input.

## Visualizers.kt { #visualizers-kt }

How to look at the audio. Every function here is an extension on a type declared elsewhere in this
category, and none of them changes what you hear.

Most of it happens without being asked for. [`registerSynthVisualizers`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt--registersynthvisualizers) runs on each new root box
and registers a value printer for [`AudioPatchSpec`](synthesis.md#fieldaudioengine-kt-audiopatchspec), [`Scope`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt-scope), [`StereoScope`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt-stereoscope), [`SpectralWavetable`](synthesis.md#spectral-kt-spectralwavetable),
[`ADSR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-adsr), [`AR`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-ar), [`BreakpointEnvelope`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-breakpointenvelope), [`EnvelopeFollower`](synthesis.md#envelopes-kt-envelopefollower), [`Compressor`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-compressor) and [`Limiter`](synthesis.md#effects-kt-limiter), so returning
one of those from a box draws it. The six envelope and dynamics types can be metered at all because
each keeps a trace of its own state as it runs; anything else has to be tapped.

Tapping means a [`Scope`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt-scope). It passes its input through untouched while recording it into a ring
buffer, so `saw.scope()` sits anywhere in a graph without altering it, and `snapshot()` lifts a
still [`AudioSnapshot`](synthesis.md#visualizers-kt-audiosnapshot) out of the ring. From a snapshot come the three renderings the file offers
everywhere: `waveformSvg`, `spectrumSvg`, and `summaryHtml` for the two side by side.

The `live*` family is those same renderings on a timer. Each starts a coroutine on the current box
that re-renders at `refreshHz`, clamped between 1 and 60, and displays into a named channel, then
returns its own receiver so the call can sit in the middle of an expression. They need a box
context and throw without one. One job is kept per box and channel, a second install cancelling the
first, and the job is registered with the box so it stops when the box does.
